docs.title: Problem, limitation or goal
docs.text: The asset and telemetry system needed a network to establish connections between endpoints, API and the server without performance bottlenecks and low processing speeds, while establishing a database that automatically sanitises SQL inputs to mitigate SQLi attacks. For our API, each endpoint must be able to communicate to the server through a secure HTTP/HTTPS connection to prevent MiTM (Man-In-The-Middle) attacks, data theft and confidentiality breaches.

docs.title: Decision (FastAPI)
docs.text: I decided to implement a RESTful API infrastructure using FastAPI, which is a highly performing, lightweight API built around the Python framework, which processes data payloads in sub-second speeds, often on par with Node.js and Go, additionally, its stateless nature, client-server seperation, cache management and layered systems allows for both client-sided (front-end) and server-sided code (back-end) to be scaled seperately from each other while being able to communicate seamlessly with each other, additionally, its cache management (determining which data is cacheable or not), allows for efficient memory namagement and minimal processing overhead.

docs.title: Decision (SQLalchemy)
docs.text: I decided to implement an Object Relational Mapper, SQLalchemyORM, with an SQLite database. This is because SQLalchemy automatically sanitises inputs without having to manually sanitise them, easily mitigating against SQLi attacks, this is done using OOP (Object Oriented Programming), representing tables as classes, inheriting from a Base class template, mitigating the use of raw SQL queries and strings. It also abstracts many database dialects such as PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and SQL Server without rewriting queries.

docs.title: Pros (FastAPI)
docs.text:
• FastAPI has speeds that nearly matches Node.js and Go, ultimately serving as the best option for our Python framework.
  • Layered systems allow for client-server interaction seamlessly while evolving on its own.
  • Efficient memory management by only cacheing specific data, rather than all data.
  • Includes self-documenting capabilities from type hints in order for developers or testers to understand our software's behaviour.
  • Includes built-in data validation using Pydantic which allows for security at the network layer.
  • FastAPI can handle concurrency with minimal processing overhead while achieving sub-second performance speeds due to its asynchronous architecture.
  • FastAPI can inject various dependency functions, allowing for efficient database management and authentication methods such as JWT tokenisation, RBAC (Role Based Access Control) and user registration/login.

docs.title: Pros (SQLalchemyORM)
docs.text:
• sqlalchemy.orm allows flexibility by tightening Python classes to database tables, columns and values. This allows for tables and relationships to be mapped seamlessly using classes, objects, inheritance, primary and foreign keys.
  • sqlalchemy.orm abstracts database dialects such as PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and SQL Server, removing the requirement to overwrite queries if you change database dialects, giving flexbility.
  • It actively protects against SQLi (SQL injection attacks) by automatically sanitising outputs when using ORMs as they treat query parameters as safe variables rather than string concatenations used from raw SQL (string concatenation is bad practise in raw SQL if done improperly, you would have to manually parameterise data such as "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = %s".)
  • It maps schemas into clean Python data structures, which allows complex data validation builds before data hits the database. This is a great advantage since FastAPI utilises a built-in data validation package Pydantic, which means we can implement data validation schemas seamlessly.

docs.title: Cons (FastAPI)
docs.text:
• async/await event handlers can freeze FastAPI's event loop under improperly implemented asynchronous events, which can lead to massive performance bottlenecks.
  • FastAPI has no standardised structure for for databases or authentication, production-level softwares must work around this by implementing their own self-configured structure which can cause "sphagetti code" if we are not careful. (Involves manually configuring database connection thread management, stateless authentication etc.)
  • Despite FastAPI's powerful dependency injections, on a large-scale, thousands of dependency functions causes debugging, testing and maintainability bottlenecks, which increases code complexity and makes sufficient code coverage less achievable.

docs.title: Cons (SQLalchemyORM)
docs.text:
• Because sqlalchemy.orm automatically turns SQL database rows/tables into heavy Python objects, the processing overhead required to do so ends up becoming an "abstraction penalty". This becomes a notable issue as the project scales, for example 10,000 queries would end up taking a significant amount of processing overhead.
  • sqlalchemy.orm relies heavily on explicit primary keys and relational constraints to track an object's state. ORMs can return inconsistent results if we decided to hook it to a previous legacy system we developed months ago, as our new system would have different primary keys (IDs unique to each column) and their own respective relational constraints, leading to heavy incompatibility.
  • If not managed properly, qeuries will be fetched sequentially one-by-one as sqlalchemy.orm, this can have severe performance bottlenecks on large-scale production software, as more queries pile up.
  • While it does create validation schemas as a Python object, more modern ORMs such as SQLModel is more compatible with Pydantic than sqlalchemy. It requires explicit configurations to achieve the same result.

docs.title: Architecture Decision Record [ADR-002]
docs.text: NOTE TO RECRUITERS: I have further amended my ADR structure to better simulate and reflect the collaborative governance of a collaborative environment, additionally, I have provided a retrospective ADR to compensate for production velocity while balancing documentation compliance. While this resulted in individual architectural decisions being bypassed during initial development phases, this allowed me to align my production velocity with my 60-day sprint without compromising system integrity.

docs.title: Title: Retrospective Formalisation of Core Asynchronous Stack & DevSecOps Architecture
docs.text:
• Status: Approved (Post-Facto Baseline)
  • Date Requested: 14 October 2026
  • Date Approved: 14 October 2026
  • Amends: None (Supersedes initial undocumented prototype phase)

docs.title: Context (Problem, Limitation or Goal)
docs.text: During the initial high-velocity prototyping phase of the Asset Management & Telemetry System, the core software components and DevSecOps isolation boundaries were implemented rapidly to verify ingestion loops. Consequently, these architectural decisions were not formally catalogued, creating minor technical and documentation debt regarding system provenance and design justification.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text: We have retrospectively baselined and approved the following architectural snapshot as the production standard for the repository: 1. API Ingestion Engine: FastAPI paired with Uvicorn to guarantee non-blocking, asynchronous execution loops (async/await) for concurrent telemetry payloads. 2. Persistence Abstraction: SQLAlchemy ORM abstraction interacting with an underlying relational database engine. 3. AppSec Verification Perimeter: Binding runtime types via strict Pydantic contract validation schemas and hard-gating commits via Bandit SAST and Pytest pipelines. 4. Docker Infrastructure: The architecture mandates dropping host root privileges by pinning a dedicated system runtime account (USER appuser) within the build schema.

docs.title: Consequences (Pros and Cons)
docs.text:
• Positive: Eliminates 100% of historical architectural documentation debt.
  • Positive: Establishes an immutable, transparent design baseline that allows future engineering contributors to understand system trade-offs instantly.
  • Positive: Establishes an airtight zero-trust sandbox boundary; if the application process is somehow compromised via a network vector, the attacker is trapped inside a low-privilege container with no path to elevate permissions on the host system.
  • Positive: Drastically accelerates onboarding velocity, allowing developers or security assessors to spin up the entire multi-layered application environment via a single, unified orchestration block (docker-compose up --build -d) rather than manually tracking system dependencies.
  • Negative: Requires a post-facto logging footprint, which temporarily impacted documentation velocity during the 60-day development sprint.
  • Negative: Introduces a migration dependency; local database session managers must eventually be re-engineered and migrated out of localized instances onto clusterised container sessions (such as a multi-container PostgreSQL architecture).
  • Negative: Heightens configurations risk; any minor mistake in the compose orchestration or port-forwarding blocks can introduce networking vulnerabilities or cause total application runtime failure.

Issue Date & Time Description Refactor 1 05/09/2618:33 Threat (Critical): Programmed two outdated packages which are abandoned (passlib.context,python-jose) in the module security.py, this can result in severe security vulnerabilities, as security keys can easily obtained or cracked, as python-jose stores the secret key internally using a raw string. Additionally, passlib.context is an abandoned package that has not received a stable release, leading to runtime errors and outdated security measures. Refactored code logic to use joserfc, a newer and more modern package that handles secret keys more securely by never storing them as a raw-string, it must be imported as a mathematically verified JWK object (JSON Web Key) before any cryptographic actions are performed. Used pwdlib instead of passlib.context as it recieves regular updates and poses minimal security risks.

docs.title: This threat model implements a component-based STRIDE analysis assuming that the attacker posesses medium-level competency (Hacker/Skilled Insider). This varies from our model in our README, which only analyses components based on primitive threats.
Unmitigated threats are being actively mitigated through our active developer backlog, for more detail, please see our Issues & Pull Requests.
docs.text:
• Spoofing: (Unmitigated) Due to the HTTPS flag being disabled (False), an attacker can perform a Man-in-the-Middle (MiTM) attack to capture unencrypted authentication tokens in transit. They can then use these stolen credentials to impersonate legitimate devices or users when communicating with the FastAPI backend.

• Tampering: (Unmitigated) Attackers can exploit logical vulnerabilities within third-party FastAPI routers or flawed validation logic to manipulate structural API payloads, tamper with database records, or alter JWT claims.

• Repudiation: (Unmitigated) Attackers may attempt to delete or alter telemetry ingestion logs (removing infection anomalies, login failures, or system events) to hide their tracks. This can be mitigated by streaming logs in real-time to an immutable, centralized logging platform that the FastAPI container cannot alter or delete.

• Information Disclosure: (Mitigated) Attackers can map out system architecture, backend dependencies, and database schemas by forcing unhandled exceptions that return verbose 500 Internal Server Error stack traces or specific try/except messages. This is mitigated by disabling FastAPI debug mode and returning unified, generic errors to the user.

• Denial of Service: (Unmitigated) Attackers can target the resource-heavy /api/telemetry/submit endpoint, rapidly sending telemetry logs to exhaust Uvicorn/Python worker processes and crash the server application.

• Elevation of Privilege: (Unmitigated) If the application container runs with root privileges or misconfigured Linux capabilities, an attacker who successfully achieves Remote Code Execution (RCE) via a framework flaw will automatically inherit root-level control over the environment.

docs.title: Why not analyse high-level attackers?
docs.text:
Even if our product is pushed to production, it does not mean our system will be targeted by state-sponsored attackers. Our system will be attacked depending on its profile, and how large its infrastructure is and what it solves.

For example, if our asset and telemetry system tracks devices across the the world internationally or regionally across a country, then there is a necessity to do so. Because our threat profile is so high, we must account for those potential security risks and vulnerabilities.

BUT. If our system only tracks about 10,000 devices in a specific area, or sparsed out, then its profile is smaller, and only would be a target for smaller and medium-level attackers.
